The Dufresni volute (Zidona dufresnii) exhibits a distinctive life history pattern among neogastropods, with ontogenetic development beginning at a remarkably small size. Neonate shells measure just 0.73 cm [Lb = 0.73 cm] in length at birth, a value derived from comparative morphometric analyses with the congeneric species Adelomelon beckii, whose hatchling shell length is proportionally similar relative to adult size. This minute initial dimension, which constrains the early feeding capabilities of the larva, necessitates a rapid transition to planktotrophy to sustain growth and ultimately influences the extended juvenile period observed in this species. The volute demonstrates a clear pattern of sexual maturation that is tightly coupled with shell size rather than chronological age, with females attaining reproductive capability upon reaching a shell length of 12.5 cm [Lp = 12.5 cm] at puberty. This pubertal threshold represents a significant proportion of the ultimate size achieved by adult snails, reflecting an extended juvenile phase during which energy is allocated predominantly to body growth rather than gamete production. Field surveys conducted along the coastal waters of the southwestern Atlantic have provided detailed morphometric data on this species, confirming the consistency of these life history benchmarks across multiple populations inhabiting the Argentine shelf.

Data on reproductive output in Zidona dufresnii reveal a moderate fecundity strategy that appears to be constrained by energetic limitations at prevailing thermal conditions. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females deposit between 4 and 5 eggs per egg capsule [N_R_i = between 4 and 5 eggs per egg capsule], with capsule deposition occurring approximately once every day during the peak spawning period [F_R_i = every day during the peak spawning period]. This combination of per-event fecundity and deposition frequency yields a daily reproductive output of roughly 4 to 5 eggs per day when females are actively spawning, a rate that aligns with observations in other volutid gastropods of comparable body size. The reproductive season is relatively protracted, with egg mass deposition documented over several weeks each austral summer, although the intensity of spawning diminishes as the season progresses. Individual females may produce multiple egg masses over the course of a single breeding period, with the total seasonal fecundity dependent upon both the duration of spawning activity and the nutritional condition of the adult prior to the onset of reproduction.

The maximum achievable shell size of Zidona dufresnii has been documented through extensive surveys of museum collections and field-caught specimens, with the largest individuals attaining an ultimate shell length of 21 cm [Li = 21 cm]. This impressive dimension places the Dufresni volute among the larger representatives of its genus and reflects a growth pattern that continues well beyond the onset of sexual maturity. Consistent with the allometric scaling typical of volutids, the maximum adult wet body mass reaches 350 grams [Wwi = 350 grams], a value supported by an extended period of somatic growth that continues well after pubertal size attainment. This substantial adult mass is supported by an extended period of somatic growth that continues after the pubertal size has been reached, with individuals investing in both reproductive output and further increases in body size. The species thus exhibits a determinate growth pattern only in a relative sense, as shell accretion continues throughout life but at a diminishing rate after the achievement of asymptotic dimensions. Comparative analyses with congeners suggest that the slow attainment of this ultimate size is linked to the relatively low productivity of the temperate benthic habitats this species occupies.

Longevity in Zidona dufresnii is remarkably extended for a gastropod of its size, with maximum lifespan documented at 18 years [am = 18 years] under natural conditions at an ambient temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This lifespan is consistent with a slow-paced life history strategy characterized by delayed maturation, moderate reproductive output, and sustained somatic growth over many years. The species attains this impressive longevity through a combination of low natural mortality rates in the adult stage and the absence of major predators capable of handling its robust shell. Mark-recapture studies conducted in the San Matías Gulf have provided direct evidence of individuals persisting for over a decade and a half, with several recaptured specimens approaching the maximum recorded age. This extended lifespan allows repeated reproductive episodes across multiple breeding seasons, contributing to the overall lifetime reproductive success of the species. The thermal regime of the southwestern Atlantic shelf, with its relatively cool and stable temperatures, likely plays a key role in mediating the metabolic rates that underpin this slow pace of life.

The reproductive cycle of Zidona dufresnii is governed by a clear seasonal pattern that is synchronized with the thermal conditions and food availability characteristic of its temperate habitat. Under the stable 18 °C [T = 18 °C] conditions that typify the peak of the austral summer, female volutes achieve their maximal daily egg production, with the peak reproduction rate reflecting a combination of per-capsule fecundity and deposition frequency. This pubertal milestone, reached at 12.5 cm [Lp = 12.5 cm], is attained at a later age in colder, deeper populations along the Argentine shelf, suggesting a temperature-mediated delay in reproductive maturation that mirrors the broader latitudinal patterns observed among volutid gastropods. Following this developmental threshold, reproductive activity is concentrated in the warmer months, when phytoplankton availability is highest and planktotrophic larvae are likely to encounter sufficient food resources during their pelagic phase. The egg capsules themselves are deposited on firm substrates, where they undergo embryonic development over a period of several weeks before hatching as free-swimming veliger larvae. This reproductive strategy, combining moderately sized egg capsules with repeated deposition events, ensures that offspring are released into the water column at a time when environmental conditions are most favorable for survival and dispersal.
